**Gregor Samsa’s transformation into a giant insect in “The Metamorphosis.”**  
This opening image—an ordinary traveling salesman waking up as a monstrous vermin—has become the most recognizable symbol of Kafka’s work and is repeatedly cited in quizzes.

**Joseph K. and the inexplicable arrest in “The Trial.”**  
The protagonist’s mysterious prosecution without a stated crime defines Kafka’s exploration of opaque bureaucracy and appears in many clue sets.

**The hunger‑artist who is replaced by a panther after his death.**  
In the short story “A Hunger Artist,” the performer’s ultimate failure and the sudden substitution of a panther serve as a striking, frequently mentioned image.

**An apple lodged in the back of a character who later hears his sister Grete’s violin.**  
Both “The Metamorphosis” and “A Country Doctor” feature the apple‑in‑the‑back injury, making it a recurring motif that quiz writers love to reference.

**Grete’s violin playing and her care for her brother.**  
Grete’s desperate attempts to support Gregor with music are a vivid detail that identifies Kafka’s novella instantly.

**The parable “Before the Law” told by a priest to Josef K.**  
This short allegory, embedded in “The Trial,” is a hallmark of Kafka’s philosophical storytelling and is often quoted verbatim in clues.

**The execution machine that inscribes “BE JUST” on an officer’s back in “In the Penal Colony.”**  
The grotesque contraption and its chilling inscription are hallmark images of Kafka’s dark imagination.

**The opening chapter “The Stoker” of the unfinished novel “Amerika.”**  
Karl Rossmann’s first job as a stoker is a well‑known entry point to Kafka’s lesser‑read but frequently alluded work.

**Kafka’s 1914 letter to Max Brod requesting that only five stories be preserved.**  
The request to limit his literary legacy, mentioning the “BE JUST” story, is a notable biographical fact often used in questions.

**The short fable “A Little Fable” with the line about the Sirens’ fatal silence.**  
Its paradoxical humor and the quoted line about silence are distinctive enough to appear repeatedly in quiz clues.

**The diary entry lamenting “the end of writing” and the title “The Judgment.”**  
Kafka’s self‑referential diary and the story of Georg Bendemann’s fatal leap are classic biographical and narrative touchstones.

**The story “The Burrow” (and the related “Josephine the Singer”).**  
These later, more obscure tales are still common in advanced questions because they showcase Kafka’s continued thematic concerns.

**The unfinished novel “The Castle” and its endless attempts to meet the elusive “Klamm.”**  
The futile quest to gain access to the Castle is a central, repeatedly cited element of Kafka’s oeuvre.
